ab_blob_rock.blurb: Blob Rock is a small bolted buttress among the quartzite cliffs on the far side of Lake Louise in Banff National Park, reached by walking the lakeside trail past the water. It holds eight sport routes, mostly in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, with a couple of 5.12s and one 5.13 for strong climbers. The rock is solid and the lines are mostly steep, so it suits climbers comfortable on the 10s who want a short day with a view of the lake and mountains. The cleanest, most worn lines are easy to pick out, and the buttress has a left-leaning edge beside a tall right-hand wall.

ab_hillside_area.blurb: Hillside area is a modest set of bolted lines on the slope above Trailside crag, in the quartzite cliffs on the far shore of Lake Louise, Banff National Park. Its eight sport routes are friendly: one around 5.8, one 5.9, and the rest in the 5.10 range, with a few of them two pitches long. That makes it a decent stop for climbers building toward the 10s who want to add something to a day at the back of the lake. It sits uphill from Trailside crag, so plan to hike up from there.

ab_sector_six.blurb: Sector Six is a single boulder in the Big Choss field under Yamnuska in the Bow Valley, holding eight limestone problems. The grades are spread widely: a handful of easy to middle problems from about V2 to V4, a pair around V7, and one very hard line near V9, so it rewards both moderate climbers and strong ones. The stone is solid and the setting is pleasant. To find it, leave the main path just before the first boulder in the field, head uphill on the branch that goes right, and keep right at each fork in the trees.

ab_graffiti_wall.blurb: Graffiti Wall is a sport wall up Carrot Creek in the Bow Valley, reached by following the creek upstream into the canyon and keeping the wall on your left. It has eight bolted routes, with one in the 5.10 range, five at 5.11 and two at 5.12, so it is aimed at climbers already comfortable leading in the 11s. The stone is solid and mostly close to vertical. The left side catches morning sun, and at least one line holds sun until mid-afternoon. Creek crossings along the way can change from year to year, so expect some wet feet or deadfall hopping.

ab_the_ledge.blurb: The Ledge is a narrow, raised shelf at Sunshine Rock, the roadside sport crag west of Banff. Eight bolted routes run from about 5.7 to 5.10, with the bulk around 5.9 and 5.10, so it works for newer leaders and for moderate mileage. The lines were put up in 2011 and see fewer climbers than the rest of the crag, so the rock is less polished and the shelf is generally quieter. The ledge itself is only a little over a metre wide, so space is limited with a big group. A short fourth-class scramble from the base of the neighbouring wall gets you up to it.
ab_the_ledge.approach: From the base of the paddock wall, scramble up and left a few metres to the ledge, which sits between the paddock and Rathaus walls.

ab_wasted_youth_wall.blurb: Wasted Youth Wall is a section of the Lost Boys crag south of Jasper, on the right side of the Main Wall. It has eight routes, almost all bolted with a single trad line, on quartzite. Grades start near 5.8 and 5.9, then cluster in the 5.10s, with a couple of 5.11s and one 5.12 on top, so it suits a party that leads 5.10 and wants a few harder options. The crag as a whole is steep, usually with the crux at an overhang, and the zone has no tourists and no lake in sight.
ab_wasted_youth_wall.parking_note: Drive Highway 93A south of Jasper and leave the car in the small gravel pull-off just before Leech Lake; there is room for very few vehicles.

ab_aspen_beauty.blurb: Aspen Beauty is a sector of the Lost Boys crag south of Jasper, and the first part of the cliff with routes taller than about ten metres. Eight lines are on offer, a mix of mostly sport with a pair of trad or top-rope lines, on quartzite. Grades run from the 5.7 to 5.8 range up through several 5.10s to a couple of 5.11s, giving a friendly spread for a climber who leads in the lower to middle 10s. To reach it, follow the base of the cliff for roughly five minutes past the first couple of short bolted lines, until the routes get taller and clean.
ab_aspen_beauty.approach: Walk along the base of the cliff for about five minutes, past the first few short bolted routes, until the routes become cleaner and about 12 m tall.
ab_aspen_beauty.parking_note: Drive Highway 93A south of Jasper and leave the car in the small gravel pull-off just before Leech Lake; there is room for very few vehicles.

ab_morro_bluffs.blurb: Morro Bluffs is a limestone sport area in Jasper National Park, on the hillside above the Athabasca River near the Morro Slabs. Its eight routes sit between about 5.7 and 5.9, are just under 30 m tall, and include a couple of two-pitch lines, so it works well for someone learning to lead on well-protected rock. Expect a walk on the Morro Slabs trail that takes roughly 15 to 20 minutes before a worn path leads off to the base of the cliff. The surrounding area is described as fairly dry and somewhat breezy.
